messages.content: Tell me the story of the evening Mullá Ḥusayn first met the Báb in Shíráz — what happened that night of His declaration?

perplexity.text:
On the evening of **22 May 1844**, Mullá Ḥusayn arrived at the gate of Shíráz after searching throughout Persia for the Promised One. There he encountered a radiant young merchant wearing a green turban—Siyyid ʿAlí-Muḥammad, later known as the Báb—who greeted him warmly, as though they were old friends, and invited him to His home.[2]

Mullá Ḥusayn initially hesitated because his companions were waiting for him, but the young man assured him that God would protect them. At the house, the Báb asked whom he was seeking. Mullá Ḥusayn described the signs taught by his spiritual master, Siyyid Káẓim: the Promised One would be of the lineage of Fáṭimih, between twenty and thirty years old, of medium height, and possess divinely given knowledge rather than learning acquired from books.[1][8]

The Báb then declared that all those signs were present in Him. Mullá Ḥusayn remained cautious and presented a difficult theological treatise connected with the teachings of Siyyid Káẓim. The Báb answered its questions with extraordinary insight. He then took up a pen and, with remarkable speed, began writing a commentary on the Súrih of Joseph—the *Qayyúmu’l-Asmá’*, regarded as the first major revealed work of the Báb.[1][2]

At **two hours and eleven minutes after sunset**, Mullá Ḥusayn recognized that his long search had ended. The Báb announced that He was the Promised One and said that this very hour would one day be commemorated.[8][10] The conversation continued until dawn, when the Báb addressed him:

> “O thou who art the first to believe in Me! Verily I say, I am the Báb, the Gate of God, and thou art the Bábu’l-Báb, the gate of that Gate.”[2][8]

The Báb then instructed him not to proclaim the news immediately. Eighteen souls, He said, had to recognize Him independently and without being summoned; these became the **Letters of the Living**, the first followers of the new revelation.[2][5]

Thus, in the quiet upper room of a modest house in Shíráz, the Báb’s declaration began—not with a public announcement, but with an all-night encounter between the Báb and the first person to recognize Him.

current.text:
The Báb declared His Mission to Mullá Ḥusayn-i-Bushrú'í in the upper room of His house in Shíráz on the evening of 22 May 1844. The Báb Himself gives the hour as two hours and eleven minutes after sunset ([Sacred Acts, Sacred Space, Sacred Time](https://bahai-library.com/6986)). Shoghi Effendi calls it "the opening scene of the initial act of this great drama" ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_26&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_3h.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_3h.683)).

**At the gate.** Mullá Ḥusayn was a leading disciple of Siyyid Káẓim, who had told his followers to go out and seek the Promised One. A Youth met him outside the city gate and greeted him with great affection. He invited him home to rest from his journey. Mullá Ḥusayn excused himself because two companions awaited him, and the Youth replied, "Commit them to the care of God… He will surely protect and watch over them" ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_233&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_96.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_96.894)). Shoghi Effendi notes that the meeting "seemed to be purely fortuitous" ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_26&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_3h.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_3h.683)).

**The conversation.** They prayed together, and then the Host asked whom Mullá Ḥusayn regarded as Siyyid Káẓim's successor, and what signs the Promised One would have ([The Báb - The Herald of the Days](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/h-m-balyuzi_the-bab-the-herald-of-the-days#p77)). Mullá Ḥusayn listed them: pure lineage, an age between twenty and thirty, innate knowledge, and freedom from bodily deficiency ([The Báb - The Herald of the Days](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/h-m-balyuzi_the-bab-the-herald-of-the-days#p77)). The Youth answered, "Behold, all these things are manifest in me" ([A Brief Introduction to Millennial Zeal in the Nineteenth Century](https://bahai-library.com/2795)). Mullá Ḥusayn politely objected that the One sought would have vast knowledge and unsurpassed holiness. He was at once overcome by fear and remorse at having said so ([A Brief Introduction to Millennial Zeal in the Nineteenth Century](https://bahai-library.com/2795)).

**The tests.** The Báb asked again, "Might not the Person intended by Siyyid Káẓim be none other than I?" ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_241&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_9e.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_9e.2854)). Mullá Ḥusayn then offered a treatise of his own on the hidden teachings of the Shaykhí school. Within minutes the Báb "unravelled all its mysteries and resolved all its problems" ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_241&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_9e.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_9e.2854)). Then, unasked, the Báb said, "Now is the time to reveal the commentary on the Súrih of Joseph" ([The Bab: The Herald of the Day of Days](https://bahai-library.com/1641)) ([The Báb - The Herald of the Days](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/h-m-balyuzi_the-bab-the-herald-of-the-days#p83)). Mullá Ḥusayn had once asked Siyyid Káẓim for such a commentary, and he had declined ([Gate of the Heart: Understanding the Writings of the Báb](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/nader-saiedi_gate-of-the-heart-understanding-the-writings-of-the-bab#p70)). As the Báb began to reveal it, Mullá Ḥusayn recalled: "I sat spellbound by His utterance, oblivious of time and of those who awaited me… Sleep had departed from me that night. I was enthralled by the music of that voice" ([The Báb - The Herald of the Days](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/h-m-balyuzi_the-bab-the-herald-of-the-days#p89)). This was the first chapter of the Qayyúmu'l-Asmá' ([Memories of Nine Years in 'Akka](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/youness-afroukhteh_memories-of-nine-years-in-akka#p1610)). Bahá'u'lláh called that book "the first, the greatest, and mightiest of all books" of the Bábí Dispensation ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_67&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_4m.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_4m.1733)).

**The declaration.** The Báb then said: "O thou who art the first to believe in Me! Verily I say, I am the Báb, the Gate of God, and thou art the Bábu'l-Báb, the gate of that Gate." He went on to say that eighteen souls must find Him, "unwarned and uninvited", and He told Mullá Ḥusayn to keep the secret ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_250&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_9n.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_9n.1182)).

**Mullá Ḥusayn's state.** He said the Revelation "came as a thunderbolt which, for a time, seemed to have benumbed my faculties", and left him with a courage that no one could withstand: "The universe seemed but a handful of dust in my grasp" ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_28&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_3j.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_3j.960)).

**Dawn.** The interview lasted until dawn ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_26&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_3h.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_3h.683)). The Báb's wife, who lay awake in the house that night, heard His voice "conversing in the most animated manner with Mullá Ḥusayn… reading the verses to him and presenting proofs and arguments" ([Memoirs of Life with 'Abdu'l-Bahá](https://bahai-library.com/khanum_episodes_life)). Mullá Ḥusayn then went down the stairs of the upper room ([Dawn Over Mount Hira](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/marzieh-gail_dawn-over-mount-hira#p828)).

The date is sometimes given as 23 May, because the hours after sunset belong to the next day in the Islamic reckoning. Saiedi puts the meeting on "the eve of May 23" ([Gate of the Heart: Understanding the Writings of the Báb](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/nader-saiedi_gate-of-the-heart-understanding-the-writings-of-the-bab#p70)). The Bahá'í observance is held about two hours after sunset on 22 May ([Sacred Acts, Sacred Space, Sacred Time](https://bahai-library.com/6986)). The full account is in [*The Dawn-Breakers*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21308), from Mullá Ḥusayn's own words as Nabíl recorded them.

I can go on to the next day, when the eighteenth Letter of the Living arrived, if you like.

perplexity.why: The outline is accurate: the meeting at the gate, the signs, the treatise, the Qayyúmu'l-Asmá', the Bábu'l-Báb declaration and the Letters of the Living. But its citations are opaque numbers, it quotes Nabíl's own words only once, and it compresses the sequence. It also loosely says the Báb predicted that the hour would be commemorated. It never names The Dawn-Breakers or God Passes By as its source.

current.why: A vivid, well-ordered account built mainly on primary sources: Nabíl's Dawn-Breakers (in Mullá Ḥusayn's own words) and God Passes By. It quotes them directly: the Báb's words at the gate, the treatise being 'unravelled', 'thunderbolt', 'handful of dust'. It adds the hour as the Báb Himself gave it, Bahá'u'lláh's praise of the Qayyúmu'l-Asmá', the Báb's wife's testimony, and an explanation of 22 vs 23 May. Secondary scholars are used only for supporting detail. Minor slips: some quotations are routed through secondary works, and the closing offer wrongly says the eighteenth Letter of the Living arrived the next day.

messages.content: What happened at the fort of Shaykh Ṭabarsí? Walk me through the course of the siege as Nabíl tells it.

perplexity.text:
Nabíl’s account presents Shaykh Ṭabarsí as a seven-month ordeal, beginning as a defensive refuge and ending in betrayal. The principal stages are these:

1. **The defenders gather at the shrine.**  
   After conflict at Bárfurúsh, Quddús and his companions withdrew to the shrine of Shaykh Ṭabarsí and fortified it. Nabíl gives their number as a little over three hundred, with Mullá Ḥusayn among their leaders.[4]

2. **The first attacks are repulsed.**  
   Local forces and then government troops repeatedly attacked the enclosure, but the defenders made sorties and scattered them. Quddús’s counterattacks forced the besiegers to retreat on several occasions.[9]

3. **Royal forces encircle the fort.**  
   Prince Mihdí-Qulí Mírzá arrived with a larger army, later reinforced by commanders including ʿAbbás-Qulí Khán and Sulaymán Khán. The besiegers constructed barricades and trenches around the fort, gradually tightening the blockade.[3]

4. **The siege becomes an artillery war.**  
   Cannon and mortar batteries were brought up, and the fort was heavily bombarded. The defenders’ position deteriorated as their ammunition and food ran low; they even had to dig a well inside the enclosure because access to water was severely restricted.[3][6]

5. **Mullá Ḥusayn’s last sortie.**  
   On 2 February 1849, Mullá Ḥusayn led about 313 companions out of the fort at night, crying “Yá Ṣáḥibu’z-Zamán!” They broke through three successive barricades and routed the troops. During the charge, however, Mullá Ḥusayn’s horse became entangled in a tent rope. A soldier’s bullet struck him in the breast; he was carried back into the fort and died soon afterward. Nabíl records that seventy-two defenders had fallen by that day.[1][3]

6. **Quddús continues the resistance.**  
   After Mullá Ḥusayn’s death, Quddús directed further sorties. In one, Mírzá Muḥammad-Báqir and eighteen companions captured an enemy artillery tower, threw down its guns, and demolished the surrounding barricades. In another attack, he led thirty-six men out, returned with an abandoned enemy banner, and lost five companions.[2]

7. **Starvation breaks the fort’s material resistance.**  
   By early April, the defenders had exhausted their grain and rice. They slaughtered and ate their remaining horses, then survived on grass, carrion, bones, skins, and leather. Nabíl portrays this suffering as the final phase of a siege that military force alone had failed to end.[10]

8. **The surrender is secured by an oath.**  
   After prolonged resistance, the prince’s forces offered safe conduct if the defenders left the fort. The guarantee was confirmed by Qurʾāns and sworn assurances. The survivors—about 220, according to the account—therefore evacuated on 9 May 1849.[4][10]

9. **The promise is immediately broken.**  
   Once the defenders had emerged, the royal troops disarmed and attacked them. Many were massacred or dispersed despite the pledged protection. Quddús was taken to Bárfurúsh and killed there, while the surviving companions were subjected to further executions and humiliation.[2][3]

Thus, in Nabíl’s telling, the fort was not conquered by a successful assault. Its defenders repeatedly defeated the besieging army, but starvation, attrition, and finally a violated Qurʾānic guarantee brought the siege to its tragic conclusion.

current.text:
The siege of the fort of Shaykh Ṭabarsí (October 1848 to May 1849) was the defence of a shrine in the Mázindarán forest. About 300 Bábís, led first by Mullá Ḥusayn and then by Quddús, held it against royal troops. It ended when the besiegers broke a Qur'án-sworn promise and massacred them. The passages I retrieved from Nabíl cover the beginning and the end better than the middle months, so those middle months are thinner below.

**1. The march and the road to the shrine**
- Mullá Ḥusayn left Mashhad with 202 companions, unfurled the Black Standard to go to Quddús's aid, and proclaimed the Message in every village ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil)).
- At Bárfurúsh the Sa‘ídu’l-‘Ulamá’ stirred up the town against them. Nabíl says the Bábís' number, discipline and enthusiasm, and the Black Standard itself, roused his hatred ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_933&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_sm.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_sm.1633)).
- Mullá Ḥusayn held his men back, saying "Not yet," until the aggressors forced them to defend themselves ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil)). Shoghi Effendi stresses this restraint. He says Mullá Ḥusayn refused to unsheathe his sword until a crowd had blocked the way and killed seven of his companions ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_104&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_5n.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_5n.6331)).
- The escort provided by Khusraw of Qádí-Kalá turned on them. Nabíl says it seized their property, killed several, and captured others. Mullá Ḥusayn protested and refused to go further with it ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_968&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_tl.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_tl.1217)).

**2. Building the fort**
- The Bábís reached the shrine on 12 October 1848, and Mullá Ḥusayn ordered a fortress built around it ([The Báb - The Herald of the Days](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/h-m-balyuzi_the-bab-the-herald-of-the-days#p684)). Horsemen attacked the same day, and the cry of "Yá Ṣáḥibu’z-Zamán" drove them off ([Mullá Ḥusayn](https://bahai-library.com/johnson_mulla_husayn)).
- Shoghi Effendi records Bahá’u’lláh's visit. He inspected the fortifications and advised the defenders, and that advice led to Quddús's deliverance ([Shoghi Effendi, God Passes By, pgs. 36-40](https://bahai-library.com/writings/shoghieffendi/gpb/36-40.html)).
- When Quddús entered, Mullá Ḥusayn counted the companions through the gate: 312, then one more youth who ran in from Bárfurúsh, making 313 ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_1003&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_uk.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_uk.859)).

**3. The fighting**
- The chronology records sorties in December 1848, including one in which Quddús was wounded, and the completion of a well inside the fort in February 1849 ([Chronology of Persecutions of Babis and Baha'is](https://bahai-library.com/926)). This is a modern chronology that cites Nabíl, not Nabíl's own words.
- Mullá Ḥusayn's last sortie was at dawn on 2 February 1849. Before it, Nabíl says, he washed, put on new garments and wore the Báb's turban. He then rode out at midnight at the head of 313 companions ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_1063&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_w8.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_w8.846)).
- ‘Abbás-Qulí Khán shot him in the chest from a tree ([The Báb - The Herald of the Days](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/h-m-balyuzi_the-bab-the-herald-of-the-days#p688)). Nabíl heard from Mullá Ṣádiq and Mullá Mírzá Muḥammad-i-Furúghí that Quddús was alone with him for two hours and that his voice was heard answering ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_1067&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_wc.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_wc.1163)).
- ‘Abbás-Qulí Khán himself later said that anyone who had seen Mullá Ḥusayn "would have been convinced that the Chief of Martyrs (Imám Ḥusayn) had returned to earth" ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_178&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_7p.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_7p.721)).

**4. Famine**
- ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says the defenders went eighteen days without food. They lived on the leather of their shoes and then on water alone. Even so, when attacked they would "instantly spring to their feet" and drive the army back ([Memorials of the Faithful](https://oceanlibrary.com/memorials-of-the-faithful_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_34&selectionString=abdu-l-baha-memorials-of-the-faithful_en_3r.0~abdu-l-baha-memorials-of-the-faithful_en_3r.851)).
- Some, worn down by hunger and trusting the prince's assurances, left the fort. They were "instantly slain" on ‘Abbás-Qulí Khán's order ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_1107&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_xg.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_xg.503)).

**5. The oath and the betrayal**
- Shoghi Effendi summarises the end. The prince swore on the Qur'án, with the oath written on the margin of its opening súrih, to free the defenders and see them safely home. He then broke it. Some were sold as slaves, and the rest were killed by sword and spear, shot, burned or blown from cannon ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_105&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_5o.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_5o.1343)).
- Nabíl says the prince did not join Quddús as promised. He sent him to the Farrásh-Báshí's tent and had the other companions told that Quddús wanted them with him. Those who went were captured and sold as slaves, and they were the only survivors ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_1120&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_xt.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_xt.639)).
- Quddús was handed to the Sa‘ídu’l-‘Ulamá’ in Bárfurúsh and put to death after being tortured, chained and mutilated ([Shoghi Effendi, God Passes By, pgs. 41-45](https://bahai-library.com/writings/shoghieffendi/gpb/41-45.html)). The Báb, in Chihríq, was so grieved at the news that He could not write or dictate for five or six months ([Chronology: Date 1849-06-00](https://bahai-library.com/chronology/1849-06-00&sort=date-asc)).

Nabíl also records the torture of Mullá Muḥammad-i-Mu‘allim-i-Núrí. The prince offered him release and a post as tutor if he would curse Quddús, and he refused ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_1323&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_13g.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_13g.946)).

I can go further into any phase, such as Quddús's trial before the ‘ulamá or the Guardian's own assessment of the episode. The full text of [*The Dawn-Breakers*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21308) is in the library.

perplexity.why: A tells the siege clearly, stage by stage, and covers the middle months well: the tower captured by Mírzá Muḥammad-Báqir's party, the famine diet and the surrender under oath. But its numbered references point to nothing, and it quotes Nabíl's own words almost nowhere. The sequence is muddled in places: early sorties are credited to Quddús, the commanders are run together, and the artillery is placed loosely. It leaves out Bahá'u'lláh's visit, Quddús's arrival and the count of 313, and some figures (about 220 survivors, 36 men) are doubtful.

current.why: B rests mainly on Nabíl, with linked passages: the march from Mashhad, the 'Not yet' restraint, Khusraw's treachery, the count of 313, Mullá Ḥusayn's preparation and death, Quddús's two hours alone with him, and the trick by which the companions were lured into captivity. It adds Shoghi Effendi and 'Abdu'l-Bahá in the right order of authority. It openly admits the middle months are thin, and labels the modern chronology as secondary. Weaknesses: some facts that Nabíl himself records are credited to Balyuzi or a chronology, and it says both 'dawn' and 'midnight' for the last sortie.

messages.content: How did the Báb's pilgrimage to Mecca unfold — what did He do at the Ka‘bih, and what message did He send to the Sherif of Mecca?

perplexity.text:
The Báb’s pilgrimage took place in late 1844. He traveled from Shiraz to Bushihr, sailed to Jeddah, and then proceeded to Mecca with Quddús. There He performed the prescribed rites of the ḥajj, observing the customary practices of the pilgrimage.[1][5]

At the Kaʿbih, after completing the rites, the Báb seized the ring of the door and proclaimed three times, in a clear voice:

> “I am that Qá’im whose advent you have been awaiting.”[1][7]

The declaration was made before the assembled pilgrims, publicly asserting His identity as the Promised One of Islam.[2]

He then composed an epistle to the Sherif of Mecca. In it, He explained the distinctive features of His mission, proclaimed the advent of His Revelation, and invited the Sherif to arise and accept His Cause. The Báb entrusted the letter, together with selections from His other writings, to Quddús for delivery.[6]

The Sherif did not respond: the message was ignored at the time, reportedly because he was preoccupied with his affairs. Later accounts state that he recognized the gravity of having disregarded the Báb’s summons, but only after the Báb’s martyrdom.[6][9]

current.text:
The Báb made the pilgrimage in 1844–45 with Quddús. At the Ka‘bih He declared Himself the Qá’im. He then sent the Sherif of Mecca an epistle, carried by Quddús, which the Sherif ignored.

**The journey.** Shoghi Effendi says He sailed from Búshihr on the 19th of Ramaḍán (October 1844), with Quddús, on a sailing vessel. He landed at Jaddih after a stormy voyage of over a month ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_35&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_3q.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_3q.1289)). At Jaddih He put on the pilgrim's garb and rode a camel to Mecca. Quddús walked all the way holding the camel's bridle ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_409&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_e2.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_e2.607)). On the tenth of Dhi'l-Ḥijjah He sacrificed nineteen lambs: nine for Himself, seven for Quddús and three for Mubárak ([The Báb - The Herald of the Days](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/h-m-balyuzi_the-bab-the-herald-of-the-days#p274)). Shoghi Effendi explained that He did this before He had revealed His own laws, when Islamic practice was not yet abrogated ([Lights of Guidance](https://oceanoflights.org/lights-of-guidance-baha-i-ocean-en/#:~:text=As%20regards%20your%20question,%7Bid%3D%22para5885%22%20ilmid%3D%22bl3sb%22%20type%3D%22par%22%20language%3D%22en%22%7D)).

**At the Ka‘bih.** Nabíl says the Báb performed all the prescribed rites with great dignity. In the intense heat He would not take off His turban or cloak, out of reverence ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_416&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_e9.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_e9.554)). Balyuzi quotes Ḥájí Mírzá Ḥabíbu'lláh-i-Afnán, who is relaying Ḥájí Abu'l-Ḥasan. After the rites, with the Ka‘bih's court and the nearby rooftops crowded with pilgrims, the Báb stood against the building. He took hold of the ring on its door and called out three times in a clear voice ([The Báb - The Herald of the Days](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/h-m-balyuzi_the-bab-the-herald-of-the-days#p275)): "I am that Qá'im whose advent you have been awaiting" ([The Bab: The Herald of the Day of Days](https://bahai-library.com/1641)). A hush fell over the crowd, but its full meaning was probably lost on them ([The Bab: The Herald of the Day of Days](https://bahai-library.com/1641)).

**The challenge to Muḥíṭ.** Shoghi Effendi names this as one of the two important episodes of the Ḥijáz visit ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_36&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_3r.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_3r.867)). Near the Black Stone, the Báb took the hand of the Shaykhí leader Mírzá Muḥíṭ-i-Kirmání. He told him that no one else, in East or West, could claim to be the Gate to the knowledge of God ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_417&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_ea.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_ea.1337)).

**The message to the Sherif.** Shoghi Effendi calls this the second episode. It was an invitation "in the form of an Epistle, conveyed by Quddús," calling on the custodian of the House of God "to embrace the truth of the new Revelation." The Sherif, absorbed in his own pursuits, did not respond ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_36&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_3r.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_3r.867)). Nabíl adds that the Báb wrote it after the last rites of the pilgrimage. It set out "in clear and unmistakable terms" the distinguishing features of His mission, and He gave it to Quddús together with selections from His other writings ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_426&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_ej.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_ej.2768)). Balyuzi calls it the Báb's last act in Mecca ([The Báb - The Herald of the Days](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/h-m-balyuzi_the-bab-the-herald-of-the-days#p288)).

**Afterward.** Shoghi Effendi says the Sherif was told about the Báb's mission and martyrdom seven years later, in a conversation with Ḥájí Níyáz-i-Baghdádí ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_36&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_3r.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_3r.867)). The library's copy of Nabíl's text cuts off before the Sherif's own words, so I can't quote them. The Báb's visit to Medina ended the pilgrimage. Back in Búshihr He said farewell to Quddús and foretold that Quddús would die a martyr and that He would later meet the same fate ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_37&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_3s.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_3s.365)).

I can look further into the Báb's exchange with Mírzá Muḥíṭ, or into what He revealed for him, if you'd like.

Its citation markers point to no sources, and it leaves out the Muḥíṭ episode and Shoghi Effendi's framing of the visit. Its closing remark about the Sherif's later response is vague and has no source.

current.why: Rests on primary accounts, God Passes By and The Dawn-Breakers, with Balyuzi clearly labelled as passing on an oral account through Afnán. It covers the voyage, the rites, the declaration, the challenge to Muḥíṭ, the epistle and its delivery, Níyáz's later conversation with the Sherif, and the farewell to Quddús. It says honestly where the text it had cut off, and invites further study. The Lights of Guidance point about the sacrifice is a small aside that could not be checked.

messages.content: Describe the Báb's examination before the ‘ulamás of Tabríz: who questioned Him, what was He asked, and how did He answer?

perplexity.text:
The Báb was examined at the governor’s residence in Tabríz before the heir to the throne, Náṣiri’d-Dín Mírzá, and a gathering of leading clerics. The principal questioner was **Ḥájí Mullá Maḥmūd, the Niẓámu’l-ʿUlamá**, tutor to the crown prince; among the other prominent divines present were **Mullá Muḥammad-i-Mamaqānī**, **Mírzā Aḥmad the Imām-Jumʿih**, and **Mírzá ʿAlí-Aṣghar, the Shaykhu’l-Islām of Tabríz**.[1][3][5]

The Niẓámu’l-ʿUlamá asked Him, in substance:

- **Who are You, and what claim do You make?**
- **What message have You brought?**
- **What proof can You offer for Your mission?**

The Báb answered emphatically:

> “I am, I am, the Promised One!”

He explained that He was the One whose advent Muslims had invoked and awaited for a thousand years, and declared that the peoples of East and West were required to obey His word.[1][2][5]

When asked for proof, He replied that **the greatest proof of a divine Messenger is His own revealed Word**. He added that He could reveal, in two days and two nights, verses equal in number to the Qur’án.[2][5]

At the Niẓámu’l-ʿUlamá’s request, the Báb then began describing the proceedings in language resembling the Qur’án. **Mullá Muḥammad-i-Mamaqānī interrupted, criticizing what he called a grammatical error.** The Báb answered that God’s Word cannot be constrained by grammatical rules devised by human beings; rather, those rules had themselves been derived from revealed Scripture. He further pointed to similar departures from conventional grammar in the Qur’án.[1][2][3]

Some accounts also record that the clerics asked Him learned questions, including one concerning the stars and planets. The Báb replied that He had not studied astronomy or astrology, and that such knowledge flowed from Him spontaneously, like His revealed verses.[4]

current.text:
The Báb was examined in Tabríz in 1848. The Crown Prince Náṣiri'd-Dín Mírzá was present, and Ḥájí Mullá Maḥmúd, the Niẓámu'l-‘Ulamá, presided. The Báb used the occasion to declare His claim openly.

**Who questioned Him**

- Ḥájí Mírzá Áqásí ordered the clergy of Tabríz to convene in the governor's residence, to arraign the Báb and find ways to end His influence ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_899&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_ro.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_ro.1184)).
- Shoghi Effendi names the Prince as heir to the throne and governor of Áḏhirbáyján. He names the Niẓámu'l-‘Ulamá, the Prince's tutor, as president. The other attendees were the leading ecclesiastics of Tabríz, the Shaykhí leaders, the Shaykhu'l-Islám and the Imám-Jum‘ih ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_63&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_4i.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_4i.1191)).
- The most prominent accusers were Mullá Muḥammad-i-Mámáqání, Mírzá ‘Alí-Aṣg̱har the Shaykhu'l-Islám, and Mírzá Aḥmad the Imám-Jum‘ih ([A Traveler’s Narrative](https://oceanlibrary.com/travelers-narrative_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_46&selectionString=abdu-l-baha-traveler-s-narrative-ocean_en_41.0~abdu-l-baha-traveler-s-narrative-ocean_en_41.765)). Balyuzi adds Ḥájí Murtiḍá-Qulí, the ‘Alamu'l-Hudá ([The Báb - The Herald of the Days](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/h-m-balyuzi_the-bab-the-herald-of-the-days#p530)).
- Historians date the event to July 1848, three months after the Báb was moved from Máh-Kú to Chihríq ([Shaykh Hasan-i-Zunuzi: The Promises Fulfilled](https://bahai-library.com/shahrokh_shaykh_hasan_zunuzi)). Nicolas thought it happened earlier, but Balyuzi, Amanat and MacEoin place it later ([A Prophet in Modern Times](https://bahai-library.com/terry_nicolas_prophet_modern)).

**What He was asked, and how He answered**

1. **Who He was.** The Báb took the one empty seat, the one reserved for the Valí-‘Ahd, and a deep silence fell. The Niẓámu'l-‘Ulamá then asked: "Whom do you claim to be… and what is the message which you have brought?" ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_901&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_rq.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_rq.2396)) The Báb answered three times: "I am, I am, the promised One! I am the One whose name you have for a thousand…" ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_901&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_rq.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_rq.2396)). The full declaration continues that they had risen at His mention and prayed for the hour of His Revelation [ ([I Shall Come Again, Volume I: Time Prophecies of the Second Coming](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/hushidar-motlagh-ed_i-shall-come-again-volume-i-time-prophecies-of-the-second-coming#p2462))].
2. **The reprimand.** Shoghi Effendi says the assembly dropped their heads in confusion. Mullá Muḥammad-i-Mámáqání then rebuked the Báb "as a perverse and contemptible follower of Satan." The Báb replied that He maintained what He had already asserted ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_64&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_4j.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_4j.1465)).
3. **Proof.** Asked for evidence, the Báb said His words were "the most incontrovertible evidence of His mission." He adduced Qur'ánic verses and claimed He could reveal, in two days and two nights, verses equal to the whole Qur'án ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_64&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_4j.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_4j.1465)). 'Abdu'l-Bahá's account has Him reciting texts and saying, "This is the permanent and most mighty proof" ([A Traveler’s Narrative](https://oceanlibrary.com/travelers-narrative_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_46&selectionString=abdu-l-baha-traveler-s-narrative-ocean_en_41.0~abdu-l-baha-traveler-s-narrative-ocean_en_41.765)).
4. **A test of revelation.** According to Balyuzi, the Niẓámu'l-‘Ulamá asked Him to describe the gathering in Qur'án-like language, so the Prince and divines could bear witness ([The Báb - The Herald of the Days](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/h-m-balyuzi_the-bab-the-herald-of-the-days#p559)).
5. **Grammar.** The divines criticized His Arabic. He answered by citing Qur'ánic passages containing the same supposed infractions ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_64&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_4j.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_4j.1465)), ([A Traveler’s Narrative](https://oceanlibrary.com/travelers-narrative_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_46&selectionString=abdu-l-baha-traveler-s-narrative-ocean_en_41.0~abdu-l-baha-traveler-s-narrative-ocean_en_41.765)). In one retelling He then ended the session by reciting a Qur'ánic verse and leaving without being dismissed ([Shaykh Hasan-i-Zunuzi: The Promises Fulfilled](https://bahai-library.com/shahrokh_shaykh_hasan_zunuzi)).

**Aftermath**

Shoghi Effendi calls the examination a "landmark" and the Báb's "supreme opportunity" to assert His claims publicly, "formally and without any reservation" ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_63&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_4i.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_4i.1191)). He also calls the interrogatory "carefully staged and farcical" ([The Promised Day is Come](https://oceanlibrary.com/promised-day-is-come_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_21&selectionString=the_promised_day_is_come_bahai_ocean_en-bl3d.0~the_promised_day_is_come_bahai_ocean_en-bl3d.1172)).

The Báb was then taken back to the house of the farrásh-báshí. The next day He was sentenced to the bastinado ([A Traveller's Narrative Written to Illustrate the Episode of the Bab](https://bahai-library.com/browne_abdul-baha_travellers_narrative&chapter=14)). The farrásh guards refused to carry it out, and the Shaykhu'l-Islám administered it himself ([The Báb - The Herald of the Days](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/h-m-balyuzi_the-bab-the-herald-of-the-days#p566)). The chronology notes that the clergy also issued a death fatwa, which the civil authorities did not enforce ([Chronology: Date 1848-07-30](https://bahai-library.com/chronology/1848-07-30)).

An English physician, Dr. Cormick, was sent to judge whether the Báb was sane. He said the Báb would answer almost none of his questions ([Uncompiled Published Letters](https://oceanlibrary.com/uncompiled-published-letters_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_2756&selectionString=published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl2f9.0~published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl2f9.2393)).

Mámáqání later recognized the Báb and said he had written a death warrant on the day of this gathering ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_1565&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_1a6.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_1a6.435)).

My searches did not turn up the whole of Shoghi Effendi's closing sentence on the Báb's departure. A reader should not treat that detail as confirmed here beyond the retelling cited above.

I can set the Dawn-Breakers account beside Balyuzi's, or look at what MacEoin's article on the "trial" says about the Persian sources.

It covers the main participants, the questions, the 'I am, I am, the Promised One' declaration, the proof from revealed verses and the grammar exchange. But its footnote markers [1]–[5] point to no listed sources, it gives no primary texts beyond one quotation, and the astronomy detail is credited only to 'some accounts' without saying which.

current.why: The answer is built on primary accounts: Nabíl, Shoghi Effendi's God Passes By and 'Abdu'l-Bahá's Traveller's Narrative. Balyuzi and the dating debate are clearly labelled as scholarly context. It quotes the key exchanges and also covers the aftermath and later significance. The Cormick passage and the closing caveat are somewhat padded or awkward, but the substance is much richer and well sourced.

messages.content: What is the story of the 'Sifter of Wheat' in Iṣfahán in the Dawn-Breakers, and why is it remembered?

perplexity.text:
In *The Dawn-Breakers*, the “Sifter of Wheat” is identified in later notes as **Mullá Jaʿfar**, commonly called **Gandum-Pák-Kun**. He was a humble wheat sifter in Iṣfahán and the **first person in the city to accept the Báb’s message**. He served Mullá Ḥusayn devotedly and became an ardent supporter of the new faith.[1][2]

When he later heard about the siege of Shaykh Ṭabarsí, he immediately set out to join the Báb’s defenders, still carrying his sieve. When asked why, he said he intended to “sift” the people he met along the way—finding those willing to embrace the Cause and accompany him to martyrdom.[1]

He eventually joined the defenders and was killed at Shaykh Ṭabarsí.[3] His story is remembered because it contrasts **humble spiritual insight with the failure of Iṣfahán’s celebrated scholars**: although the city was renowned for learning and religious institutions, the Báb said that only this ordinary laborer recognized the truth and received the “robe of Divine virtue.”[1] The sieve thus became a symbol of discernment, wholehearted faith, and the principle that spiritual greatness is not determined by social rank or scholarly reputation.

current.text:
The "Sifter of Wheat" was Mullá Muḥammad Ja‘far Gandum-Pák-Kun. He was the first person in Iṣfahán to accept the Báb, and he later died defending the Fort of Shaykh Ṭabarsí ([The Kitáb-i-Aqdas](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-aqdas_bahaullah?paraId=fn_183)).

**The story in *The Dawn-Breakers*.** Nabíl writes that he was the first in Iṣfahán to embrace the Cause. As soon as the Call reached him, he "unreservedly accepted the Message". He served Mullá Ḥusayn with "marvellous devotion" and became a zealous advocate of the new Revelation ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_323&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_bo.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_bo.1588)). A few years later he heard the details of the siege of the fort of Shaykh Ṭabarsí. He felt an "irresistible impulse" to join its defenders, took his sieve in his hand, and set out. The library's text breaks off there, so I can't quote the rest of his reply. Other retellings give it as saying he carried the sieve to "sift" the people of each city he passed ([Mullá Ḥusayn](https://bahai-library.com/johnson_mulla_husayn)). According to the Kitáb-i-Aqdas notes, he joined the defenders and perished during the siege ([The Kitáb-i-Aqdas](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-aqdas_bahaullah?paraId=fn_183)).

**Why he is remembered.**

1. **The Báb named him.** In the Persian Bayán the Báb wrote that Iṣfahán was full of seminaries and men "regarded as divines and doctors" ([Selections from the Writings of the Báb](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-the-bab/?paraId=para_402&selectionString=selections_from_the_writings_of_the_bab_bahai_en-blc0.0~selections_from_the_writings_of_the_bab_bahai_en-blc0.581)). Yet when the time came for inmost essences to be drawn forth, "only its sifter of wheat donned the robe of discipleship." The Báb adds that this is the mystery of the saying that "the abased shall be exalted and the exalted shall be abased" ([Selections from the Writings of the Báb](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-the-bab/?paraId=para_402&selectionString=selections_from_the_writings_of_the_bab_bahai_en-blc0.0~selections_from_the_writings_of_the_bab_bahai_en-blc0.581)). In the Báb's account, learned Iṣfahán rejected the Message and only one man recognised the Truth ([The Bab: The Herald of the Day of Days](https://bahai-library.com/1641)).

2. **Bahá'u'lláh alluded to him.** Paragraph 166 of the Kitáb-i-Aqdas refers to "a sifter of wheat and barley" ([The Kitáb-i-Aqdas](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-aqdas_bahaullah)). The Aqdas notes identify this as an allusion to Mullá Ja‘far ([The Kitáb-i-Aqdas](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-aqdas_bahaullah)). I did not retrieve the text of that paragraph itself.

3. **He shows that rank and learning do not decide who recognises a Manifestation.** The Báb sets the humble tradesman against the city's learned clergy ([Selections from the Writings of the Báb](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-the-bab/?paraId=para_402&selectionString=selections_from_the_writings_of_the_bab_bahai_en-blc0.0~selections_from_the_writings_of_the_bab_bahai_en-blc0.581)). Mullá Ḥusayn had a friendly reception from several prominent figures in Iṣfahán, but none of them accepted the Faith at that point. Others, such as Mírzá Muḥammad-‘Alíy-i-Nahrí and Mullá Ṣádiq, followed later ([The Bab: The Herald of the Day of Days](https://bahai-library.com/1641)) ([The Bab: The Herald of the Day of Days](https://bahai-library.com/1641)).

Salmání, who knew Iṣfahán's Bábís, also recalls him as "a miller, also a Bábí, who is famous as the Sifter of Wheat." He notes that several Iṣfahán Bábís went to the fort ([My Memories of Baha'u'llah](https://bahai-library.com/salmani_memories_bahaullah)).

The story is told in [*The Dawn-Breakers*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21308). I can look for the Aqdas paragraph itself or Nabíl's account of Shaykh Ṭabarsí if you'd like.

messages.content: How was the Báb martyred in Tabríz in 1850? What happened with the first volley and Sám Khán's regiment?

perplexity.text:
The Báb was executed in Tabríz on **9 July 1850**. He and His companion, **Mírzá Muḥammad-‘Alí—known as Anís**, were suspended by ropes from a nail in the wall of the barracks square. About **750 soldiers** of the Armenian Christian regiment of Urúmíyyih, commanded by **Sám Khán**, fired in three successive volleys.[2][5]

When the smoke cleared, Anís was still alive and unharmed, while the Báb had disappeared from the wall. The bullets had severed the ropes without injuring either man; the Báb was then found back in the room where He had been held, completing a conversation with His secretary.[3][5]

Sám Khán was deeply shaken and refused to fire again or allow his regiment to participate further. He withdrew his men, reportedly declaring that he would not undertake an act that might harm the Báb, even at the cost of his own life.[3][8] A second regiment, commanded by **Áqá Ján Khán-i-Khamsih**, was brought in. The Báb and Anís were suspended again, and the subsequent volley killed them; their bodies were severely shattered.[4][5]

current.text:
The Báb was shot by firing squad on 9 July 1850 (noon) in the barracks square of Tabríz. The first volley left Him unharmed and cut only the ropes. The Armenian regiment under Sám Khán then refused to fire again, and a second regiment carried out the execution.

**The setting.** The chronology gives the date as noon on 9 July 1850. The Báb and His companion Mírzá Muḥammad-‘Alí Zunúzí, called Anís, were suspended on a wall in the square before the citadel ([Chronology: Date 1850-07-09-01](https://bahai-library.com/chronology/1850-07-09-01&sort=event-desc)). Shoghi Effendi writes that a spike was driven into a pillar between two rooms of the barracks facing the square. The Báb and Anís were hung separately from two ropes fastened to it ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_125&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_68.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_68.776)).

**Sám Khán's hesitation.** Sám Khán was colonel of the Armenian Christian regiment. Balyuzi says he was ill at ease and went to the Báb. He said he was a Christian with no ill will toward Him, and asked that, if His Cause were true, he be freed from the obligation to shed His blood. The Báb answered: "Follow your instructions, and if your intention be sincere, the Almighty is surely able to relieve you from your perplexity." ([The Báb - The Herald of the Days](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/h-m-balyuzi_the-bab-the-herald-of-the-days#p622))

**The first volley.** The squad stood in three files of 250 men, and each file fired in turn. The smoke from 750 rifles was so dense that it darkened the sky ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_125&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_68.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_68.776)). When it cleared, the crowd of about ten thousand saw that the Báb "had vanished from their sight." Anís stood alive and unhurt beside the wall, and only the ropes were severed ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_126&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_69.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_69.738)). The Báb was found "unhurt and unruffled" in the room He had occupied the night before. He was finishing His interrupted conversation with His amanuensis, Siyyid Ḥusayn ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_126&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_69.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_69.738)). He greeted the farrásh-báshí: "I have finished My conversation with Siyyid Ḥusayn… Now you may proceed to fulfill your intention." ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_126&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_69.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_69.738)) This fulfilled what He had told the farrásh-báshí earlier, that no earthly power could silence Him until He had said all He wished to say ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_124&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en-blw8.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en-blw8.955)). The farrásh-báshí left the scene and resigned his post ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_126&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_69.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_69.738)).

**Sám Khán's regiment.** Sám Khán remembered the Báb's reassuring words and ordered his men out of the barracks. He swore never to repeat the act, even at the cost of his life ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_127&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_6a.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_6a.874)). Nabíl gives the same account: Sám Khán refused ever again to involve himself or his regiment in any injury to the Báb ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_1578&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_1aj.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_1aj.311)).

**The second volley.** Áqá Ján-i-Khamsih, colonel of the bodyguard, volunteered to replace him. The Báb and His companion were hung again on the same wall in the same way. This time "their breasts were riddled with bullets." Their bodies were dissected, except for their faces, which were little marred ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_127&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_6a.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_6a.874)). Just before the volley the Báb cried out, "O wayward generation!" ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_127&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_6a.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_6a.874))

**Aftermath.** Shoghi Effendi reports that a gale and a whirlwind of dust blinded the people from noon till night. He also records that 250 of the replacement firing squad later died in an earthquake, and that the other 500 were executed three years later for mutiny ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_128&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_6b.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_6b.1016)).

'Abdu'l-Bahá was asked about Anís and the first volley. He answered that Anís was killed in the first one and mutilated, but the Báb's body "was not hit by the first volley." ([Talks of 'Abdu'l-Bahá in Haifa](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/talks-of-abdul-baha-in-haifa#p73)) This differs from Shoghi Effendi's account, in which Anís is found unharmed. Note also that Nabíl's Dawn-Breakers passage has Sám Khán sending the men out, but the replacement regiment appears in Shoghi Effendi's God Passes By.

I can also trace how the body was rescued and taken to Ṭihrán, if you'd like.

messages.content: What happened to Bahá'u'lláh at Ámul after He tried to reach Shaykh Ṭabarsí — why was He beaten there?

perplexity.text:
After setting out from Núr with companions to aid the besieged Bábís at Shaykh Ṭabarsí, Bahá’u’lláh was arrested about nine miles from the fort and taken to Ámul.[1][2]

At Ámul, the local clergy stirred up the population against the captives, portraying them as enemies of Islam and demanding severe punishment. The acting governor, fearing the mob and the clerics, ordered the prisoners to be bastinadoed—beaten on the soles of their feet.[3][4]

Bahá’u’lláh intervened to save His companions, declaring that they were innocent and offering Himself to receive the punishment in their place. He was therefore beaten alone, with rods until His feet bled, and was then subjected to further abuse from the crowd, including stones and insults.[2][6] He was beaten not because He had committed a specific crime, but as a political and religious concession intended to appease the hostile clergy and mob.

current.text:
Bahá'u'lláh was bastinadoed at Ámul because the clergy there treated Him and His companions as Bábís who were heading to join the defenders of Shaykh Ṭabarsí. The town's divines demanded their death, and the deputy-governor ordered the beating as a way to appease them.

**How He came to be at Ámul.** He had set out for the fort with some companions. The Governor of Ámul, Mírzá Taqí, learned of the plan. He surrounded the village of Níyálá at night with seven hundred riflemen and sent Bahá'u'lláh back to Ámul with eleven riders ([Memorials of the Faithful](https://oceanlibrary.com/memorials-of-the-faithful_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_712&selectionString=abdu-l-baha-memorials-of-the-faithful_en_og.0~abdu-l-baha-memorials-of-the-faithful_en_og.430)). Balyuzi adds that the Governor-General, ʻAbbás-Qulí Khán, was away at the prince's camp. His deputy was therefore the one who held the captives ([Bahá’u’lláh -- The King of Glory](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/h-m-balyuzi_bahaullah-the-king-of-glory#p210)).

**Why the beating.** ʻAbdu'l-Bahá says that Bahá'u'lláh was held in prison and then "delivered into their hands" when the ʻulamá gathered in the mosque. They "afflicted Him with a myriad torments", including the bastinado, which left His feet "sore wounded for some time" ([Light of the World](https://oceanlibrary.com/light-of-the-world_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_115&selectionString=light_of_the_world_baha_i_ocean_en-bl61.0~light_of_the_world_baha_i_ocean_en-bl61.556)).

Shoghi Effendi describes the same scene. Bahá'u'lláh received the bastinado "by order, and in the presence, of the assembled siyyids and mujtahids" to whom the civil authorities of Ámul had handed Him over ([The Promised Day is Come](https://oceanlibrary.com/promised-day-is-come_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_28&selectionString=the_promised_day_is_come_bahai_ocean_en-bl3k.0~the_promised_day_is_come_bahai_ocean_en-bl3k.1233)).

Balyuzi, drawing on Nabíl, explains the deputy-governor's motive. The divines were interrogating Bahá'u'lláh in the mosque and insisting that He and His companions be put to death as Bábís. The deputy-governor was embarrassed by this. To "hold in check the passions which had been aroused", he ordered his attendants to prepare the rods and inflict a punishment, promising to keep the captives in prison until the Governor returned ([Bahá’u’lláh -- The King of Glory](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/h-m-balyuzi_bahaullah-the-king-of-glory#p215)).

**His intervention.** Bahá'u'lláh stepped in so that His companions would not be beaten and asked that the punishment fall on Him instead. The deputy-governor, reluctantly, ordered that Bahá'u'lláh alone suffer it ([Bahá’u’lláh -- The King of Glory](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/h-m-balyuzi_bahaullah-the-king-of-glory#p215)). Balyuzi names the companions as Mullá Báqir (a Letter of the Living), Ḥájí Mírzá Jání and Mírzá Yaḥyá ([The Báb - The Herald of the Days](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/h-m-balyuzi_the-bab-the-herald-of-the-days#p687)).

**The mood in the town.** Bahá'u'lláh Himself recalled that more than four thousand people had packed the mosque and the rooftops. The leading mullá denounced Him in the Mázindarání dialect, saying He had "perverted the Faith of Islám" ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_1423&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_168.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_168.1050)).

Nabíl dates the episode to about December 1848 ([Chronology of Principal Events Related in the Dawn-Breakers](https://bahai-library.com/1645)). The mosque and school in Ámul where it happened are counted among the Bahá'í holy places of Mázandarán ([Írán: Provinces of Mázandarán and Gurgán](https://bahai-library.com/momen_encyclopedia_mazandaran)).

I can follow what happened to Him next in Ámul, or the passage in the *Epistle to the Son of the Wolf* that ʻAbdu'l-Bahá was explaining.

messages.content: Who was Quddús, and what was his role at Shaykh Ṭabarsí?

perplexity.text:
Quddús was the title of **Mullá Muḥammad-ʿAlí of Bárfurúsh**, a prominent early follower of the Báb and one of the **Letters of the Living**. The Báb chose him as His sole companion on the pilgrimage to Mecca and Medina and regarded him as one of His foremost disciples.[1][3]

At **Shaykh Ṭabarsí**, Quddús joined the Bábí defenders after being released from confinement in Sárí. He became their principal spiritual leader after Mullá Ḥusayn’s death, while others directed the fort’s military operations; thus, he provided religious authority, guidance, and moral leadership to the besieged community.[2][5][8] Following the fort’s surrender, Quddús was taken to Bárfurúsh and killed on May 16, 1849.[1][2]

current.text:
Quddús was the eighteenth and last of the Báb's Letters of the Living. At Shaykh Ṭabarsí he was the spiritual head of the besieged Bábís, and he died as a martyr soon after the siege ended.

**Who he was**
- Nabíl calls him first among the Báb's followers. He was the Báb's chosen companion on the pilgrimage to Mecca and Medina, and one of the first to suffer persecution on Persian soil ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_1143&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_yg.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_yg.992)).
- He was a native of Bárfurúsh. At eighteen he left for Karbilá, where he studied under Siyyid Káẓim for about four years. At twenty-two he recognised the Báb in Shíráz ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_1143&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_yg.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_yg.992)).
- Shoghi Effendi calls Quddús and Mullá Ḥusayn "respectively the last and the first" ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_103&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_5m.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_5m.1666)) of the Letters of the Living. Both were among the martyrs of this struggle ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_103&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_5m.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_5m.1666)).

**At Shaykh Ṭabarsí**
- Quddús was in captivity at Sárí when Mullá Ḥusayn raised the Black Standard at the Báb's command and marched with 202 companions ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil)). Shoghi Effendi says Mullá Ḥusayn was marching "to meet and lend his assistance to Quddús" ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_103&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_5m.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_5m.1666)).
- Quddús had been held for about ninety-five days. Bahá'u'lláh sent Mullá Mihdíy-i-Khu'i with six men to Sárí to demand his release, and Quddús then joined the companions at the fort ([Bahá’u’lláh -- The King of Glory](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/h-m-balyuzi_bahaullah-the-king-of-glory#p193)). The chronology dates his arrival to 27 November 1848 ([Chronology of Principal Events Related in the Dawn-Breakers](https://bahai-library.com/1645)).
- On arrival he had Mullá Ḥusayn count the companions, and the number came to 312. He said that what the Prophet had spoken about the promised One "must needs be fulfilled" ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_1003&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_uk.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_uk.859)). He asked after Bahá'u'lláh, and Mullá Ḥusayn told him Bahá'u'lláh would return to the fort later, God willing ([Mullá Ḥusayn](https://bahai-library.com/johnson_mulla_husayn)).
- Marzieh Gail says Quddús "commanded the besieged men" ([Dawn Over Mount Hira](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/marzieh-gail_dawn-over-mount-hira#p465)). Winters says Mullá Ḥusayn and Quddús were the two central figures of this uprising ([Dying for God: Martyrdom in the Shii and Babi Religions](https://bahai-library.com/winters_dying_for_god&chapter=4)). In practice Mullá Ḥusayn led the fighting and Quddús was the spiritual centre. The chronology records them leading a night attack together on the encamped army, in which Quddús was wounded in the mouth. Mullá Ḥusayn used Quddús's sword after his own broke ([Chronology: Date 1849-01-11](https://bahai-library.com/chronology/1849-01-11)).
- Shoghi Effendi notes that Quddús addressed his companions in the fort and quoted the Prophet's words: "O how I long to behold the countenance of My brethren…" ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_176&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_7n.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_7n.864)).
- When Mullá Ḥusayn fell, Quddús looked after his body himself. He put his own shirt on him and ordered his burial beside the shrine ([Quddus](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/books/johnson_quddus#p244)).

**The end**
Shoghi Effendi describes how Prince Mihdí-Qulí Mírzá swore an oath on the Qur'án to free the defenders, then broke it. The companions of Quddús were betrayed, some sold as slaves and others killed ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_105&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_5o.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_5o.1343)). Quddús was taken to Bárfurúsh, handed over to his enemy Sa'ídu'l-'Ulamá, and tortured ([The Báb - The Herald of the Days](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/h-m-balyuzi_the-bab-the-herald-of-the-days#p693)). He was martyred in the Sabzih-Maydán on 16 May 1849 ([Chronology of Principal Events Related in the Dawn-Breakers](https://bahai-library.com/1645)). In prison at Chihríq, the Báb was so overcome by grief at the news that He could not write or dictate for five or six months ([Chronology: Date 1849-06-00](https://bahai-library.com/chronology/1849-06-00)). He later revealed a Tablet of Visitation for Quddús ([Chronology: Date 1849-06-00](https://bahai-library.com/chronology/1849-06-00)).

I can go on to Nabíl's account of the Prince's betrayal, or to the Báb's Tablet of Visitation for Quddús, if you'd like.

current.why: It builds on the primary accounts first, Nabíl and God Passes By, and labels the scholars (Balyuzi, Gail, Winters) as supporting context. It is rich and accurate on the history: his arrival from Sárí, the count of 312 companions, the night sortie in which he was wounded, how he cared for Mullá Ḥusayn's body, the broken oath, his martyrdom and the Báb's grief. A few citations point to secondary chronologies instead of Nabíl directly, and one quotation's location in God Passes By may be wrong. It ends by inviting the reader to explore further.

messages.content: Who was Siyyid Káẕim-i-Rashtí, and what did he tell his disciples before his death about the Promised One?

perplexity.text:
Siyyid Káẓim-i-Rashtí (1793–1843) was the successor of Shaykh Aḥmad-i-Aḥsá’í and leader of the Shaykhí movement. He taught that the Promised One—the Qa’im or Mahdi—was already living on earth and would soon appear.[1][2]

Before his death, he urged his disciples to leave their homes, detach themselves from worldly concerns, scatter far and wide, and search for the Promised One rather than wait for him to come to them.[2][4] He described the Promised One as:

- Descended from the Prophet Muḥammad and the family of Fāṭimah
- Of noble and pure lineage
- Young—more than 20 but less than 30
- Possessed of innate knowledge
- Of medium height
- Free from bodily defects and not a smoker[1][6]

He reportedly added that he himself would not live to see the Promised One’s appearance, but that his disciples would find Him in their own lifetime.[7]

current.text:
Siyyid Káẓim-i-Rashtí was the disciple and chosen successor of Shaykh Aḥmad-i-Aḥsá'í. He led the Shaykhí school from Karbilá until his death at the end of 1843, and he prepared his followers for the coming of the Promised One.

**Who he was**
- Shoghi Effendi calls him "S̱hayḵh Aḥmad's disciple and successor" ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_208&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_8j.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_8j.695)).
- 'Abdu'l-Bahá says Shaykh Aḥmad trained him and, before he died, appointed him successor. Siyyid Káẓim then worked "night and day" explaining the inner meanings of the Qur'án. He "so imbued the people with anticipation for the coming Revelation" that his disciples, in their eagerness, dispersed in every direction until they found the Promised One ([Additional Tablets, Extracts and Talks](https://oceanlibrary.com/additional-tablets-extracts-and-talks_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_70&selectionString=abdu_l_baha_additional_tablets_extracts_and_talks_430a4c77afa01f6eb5e4f2c4028e655d_4c.0~abdu_l_baha_additional_tablets_extracts_and_talks_430a4c77afa01f6eb5e4f2c4028e655d_4c.455)).
- Shoghi Effendi notes that he wrote of the Qá'im's coming and martyrdom, and that he alluded to the name "Bahá" in his commentary on the Lámíyyih ode ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_208&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_8j.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_8j.695)).
- One account says he died on 31 December 1843 ([Mullá Ḥusayn](https://bahai-library.com/johnson_mulla_husayn)).

**What he told his disciples**
1. **Renounce the world and seek Him out.** In Nabíl's account, as his days drew to a close he exhorted them: "Beware, beware, lest after me the world's fleeting vanities beguile you... It is incumbent upon you to renounce all comfort, all earthly possessions and kindred, in your quest of Him who is the Desire of your hearts and of mine. Scatter far and wide... Never relax in your determination to seek and find Him who is concealed behind the veils of glory." ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_210&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_8j.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_8j.3031))
2. **The Advent is near.** 'Abdu'l-Bahá writes that not long before his death he told them the promised Advent was at hand. "Go forth," he repeatedly said, "and seek out your Lord." ([Memorials of the Faithful](https://oceanlibrary.com/memorials-of-the-faithful_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_690&selectionString=abdu-l-baha-memorials-of-the-faithful_en_nu.0~abdu-l-baha-memorials-of-the-faithful_en_nu.1172)) Balyuzi records the same parting counsel. They were to leave their homes, cloisters, studies and debates to seek "the Lord of the Age," whose light would soon break upon the world ([The Báb - The Herald of the Days](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/h-m-balyuzi_the-bab-the-herald-of-the-days#p68)).
3. **What would follow the Qá'im.** According to Shoghi Effendi, he declared: "Verily, I say, after the Qá'im the Qayyúm will be made manifest. For when the star of the former has set the sun of the beauty of Ḥusayn will rise and illuminate the whole world." He added that to have attained that Day "is to have attained unto the crowning glory of past generations, and one goodly deed performed in that age is equal to the pious worship of countless centuries." ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_208&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_8j.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_8j.695))

**What the disciples did**
Mullá Ḥusayn and others kept vigil for forty days in the mosque of Kúfih and then set out in different directions ([The Báb - The Herald of the Days](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/h-m-balyuzi_the-bab-the-herald-of-the-days#p68)). When Mullá Ḥusayn met the Báb in Shíráz, he answered the Báb's question about a successor by repeating this deathbed counsel. He said Siyyid Káẓim had urged them to "forsake our homes, to scatter far and wide, in quest of the promised Beloved." ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_240&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_9d.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_9d.1641))

I can go on to the signs Siyyid Káẓim gave Mullá Ḥusayn for recognizing the Promised One, if you'd like.

It adds the Qá'im/Qayyúm prophecy and Mullá Ḥusayn's later account to the Báb. Balyuzi and Johnson are correctly kept as supporting context. It leaves out the specific signs of the Promised One, though it offers to cover them.

perplexity.why: The facts are accurate, including the list of signs (lineage, age between twenty and thirty, innate knowledge, medium height, not a smoker), which matches Nabíl. But the footnotes are bare numbers with no sources behind them, it quotes nothing from the primary accounts, and it is thin. It also misses the Qayyúm prophecy and 'Abdu'l-Bahá's testimony.

messages.content: Who was Manúchihr Khán, the Mu‘tamidu'd-Dawlih, and how did he treat the Báb in Iṣfahán?

perplexity.text:
Manúchihr Khán Mu‘tamidu’d-Dawlih was the Georgian-born, Christian-born eunuch who served as governor-general of Iṣfahán under Muḥammad Shāh Qājār. Though regarded as a forceful and capable administrator, he became deeply impressed by the Báb and, according to Bahá’í accounts, accepted His message.[3][5][8]

When the Báb approached Iṣfahán in 1846, He wrote to Manúchihr Khán requesting shelter. The governor arranged for the Báb to be received respectfully in the home of Mírzá Muḥammad, the Imám-Jum‘ih, where He stayed for about forty days.[5][6][10] Manúchihr Khán then visited Him, convened a gathering of prominent divines, and invited the Báb to demonstrate the truth of Islam’s prophetic mission; the Báb’s eloquence reportedly heightened the governor’s admiration.[5]

When opposition from the clerics intensified and the Báb was ordered toward Tihrán, Manúchihr Khán protected Him rather than allowing Him to fall into hostile hands. He secretly transferred the Báb to his own residence, the Imārat-i-Khurshīd, where the Báb remained for roughly four months under the governor’s protection.[5][8] Bahá’í sources further state that Manúchihr Khán offered the Báb his wealth and military resources, and that he repented of the oppressive origins of his fortune.[4][6] His death in early 1847 ended this period of protection, after which the Báb was exposed again to official and clerical hostility.[1][4]

current.text:
Manúchihr Khán, the Mu‘tamidu'd-Dawlih ("trust of the state"), was the governor of Iṣfahán when the Báb arrived there in autumn 1846. He became the Báb's protector and one of His most prominent followers. ([Sacred Time: Babi and Baha'i History and Biography](https://bahai-library.com/6987)) ([The Babi and Bahá’í Religions 1844-1944: Some Contemporary Western Acc…](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/moojan-momen-editor_the-babi-and-bahai-religions-1844-1944-some-contemporary-western-accounts#p442))

**Who he was**
- Balyuzi calls him the Governor-General of Iṣfahán, "a Georgian eunuch." ([The Báb - The Herald of the Days](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/h-m-balyuzi_the-bab-the-herald-of-the-days#p410)) Shoghi Effendi describes him as "a Georgian by origin and a Christian by birth." ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_48&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_43.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_43.981))
- The Guardian calls him "wise and judicious" ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_48&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_43.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_43.981)). Balyuzi says he was trusted by Muḥammad Sháh ([The Báb - The Herald of the Days](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/h-m-balyuzi_the-bab-the-herald-of-the-days#p443)).
- The Mu‘tamid's title was granted by the Sháh. ([Sacred Time: Babi and Baha'i History and Biography](https://bahai-library.com/6987))

**How he treated the Báb**
1. **Lodging.** The Báb wrote to him before reaching the city asking for a lodging. ([A Traveler’s Narrative](https://oceanlibrary.com/travelers-narrative_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_28&selectionString=abdu-l-baha-traveler-s-narrative-ocean_en_3j.0~abdu-l-baha-traveler-s-narrative-ocean_en_3j.585)) The Mu‘tamid asked the Imám-Jum‘ih, Mír Siyyid Muḥammad, to receive the Báb, and the Báb stayed in the Imám's house for forty days. ([Bahá’u’lláh -- The King of Glory](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/h-m-balyuzi_bahaullah-the-king-of-glory#p1319))
2. **The interview and the commentary.** The Guardian writes that the Mu‘tamid visited the Báb before an assembly of leading divines. He asked the Báb to expound and demonstrate the truth of Muḥammad's specific mission. The divines present had felt compelled to decline, but the Báb agreed. He wrote a dissertation of about fifty pages in under two hours. ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_48&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_43.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_43.981))
3. **Public gatherings.** Nabíl records that the Mu‘tamid also held gatherings at his own home. Learned men put abstruse philosophical questions to the Báb there, including points from Mullá Ṣadrá's *‘Arshíyyih*. ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_602&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_jf.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_jf.1357))
4. **Shelter against the clergy.** Ḥájí Mírzá Áqásí suspected the Mu‘tamid's "secret sympathies." He pressed the Imám-Jum‘ih and stirred up the clergy, and the Sháh summoned the Báb to Ṭihrán. The Mu‘tamid moved the Báb into his own home. ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_50&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_45.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_45.3355))
5. **The ruse.** After the ‘ulamás condemned the Báb, the Mu‘tamid sent Him out of the city at sunset under a escort of five hundred horsemen. The escort was reduced stage by stage, and a few trusted men were to bring the Báb back in disguise before dawn. ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_610&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_jn.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_jn.1474)) ([The Bab: The Herald of the Day of Days](https://bahai-library.com/1641)) The Báb then stayed in the governor's private residence, the Imárat-i-Khurshíd. ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_621&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_jy.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_jy.1001))
6. **Honour in private.** Nabíl says the Mu‘tamid "lavished" honours on his Guest in the privacy of his home. ([The Dawn-Breakers](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_621&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_jy.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_jy.1001)) One account says he waited on the Báb in person and offered his wealth and army. The Báb replied that the Cause would triumph through "the poor and lowly" and their blood. ([History of the Báb](https://bahai-library.com/shahrokh_history_bab)) That account is by Darius Shahrokh, a later writer.

**His death and its aftermath**
He died on 4 March 1847. The Báb had predicted his death 87 days before, and the governor had left his vast holdings to the Báb. ([Chronology: Date 1847-03-04](https://bahai-library.com/chronology/1847-03-04)) His nephew and successor Gurgín Khán took everything and told the Sháh where the Báb was. ([The Báb - The Herald of the Days](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/h-m-balyuzi_the-bab-the-herald-of-the-days#p443)) The Báb was then sent toward Ṭihrán in secret. ([Chronology: Date 1847-03-04](https://bahai-library.com/chronology/1847-03-04)) That began the road to Máh-Kú and Chihríq. ([Sacred Acts, Sacred Space, Sacred Time](https://bahai-library.com/6986))

'Abdu'l-Bahá's account of how the Mu‘tamid became a believer is in ([Abdu'l-Bahá's Second European Journey](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/mirza-ahmad-sohrab_abdul-bahas-second-european-journey#p675)). I can go through it if you want.
